summary.title: The Absolute Minimum Every Software Developer Absolutely, Positively Must Know About Unicode and Character Sets (No Excuses!)
summary.one_liner: Learn why strings have no meaning without an encoding, how code points differ from byte encodings like UTF-8 and UTF-16, and how charsets are declared in email and HTML.
keywords: why does my website show gibberish
takeaways: Unicode maps each character to an abstract code point (e.g. U+0041 for A); encodings such as UTF-8 or UTF-16 define how those code points are stored as bytes.
Unicode is not simply a 16-bit code; it defines far more than 65,536 code points.
A string has no meaning without knowing its encoding; there is no such thing as plain text.
Declare the charset in email Content-Type headers or in the HTML meta tag, and place the meta tag early in the head section.
UTF-8 is backward compatible with ASCII for English text and is a common choice for publishing web pages.
summary.summary: Joel Spolsky's classic article gives a historical walk-through of character sets, from ASCII through the DOS/Windows OEM and ANSI code pages and DBCS to Unicode. It explains the distinction between abstract Unicode code points (U+XXXX) and their byte encodings, including UCS-2, UTF-16, UTF-8, UTF-7 and UCS-4. It also covers how charset information is carried in email MIME headers and HTML meta tags, and how browsers guess encodings when none is given. The author closes with his team's practice of using UCS-2 internally and publishing UTF-8.
